usage: Used when you want to provide an example to clarify a complex point in an essay or presentation.
example_sentences: By way of illustration, consider the impact of climate change on agriculture.
Not all languages are related; by way of illustration, look at Basque.
By way of illustration, the company cut costs by reducing office space.
Inflation is a complex issue; by way of illustration, examine recent food prices.
By way of illustration, many students struggle with time management during exams.
collocations: By way of illustration, let us
By way of illustration, we can
native_notes: Sounds very academic and polished. Excellent for IELTS Writing Task 2 to show lexical variety.

usage: Used to show a sharp difference between two distinct points or groups of data.
common_mistakes: Using it to compare identical things
example_sentences: Urban areas grew rapidly; by contrast, rural populations declined.
He loves action films. By contrast, his sister prefers documentaries.
The first study found positive results. By contrast, the second study failed.
Public transport is cheap. By contrast, owning a car is expensive.
By contrast with last year, the company's profits have doubled.
native_notes: Best used when comparing two specific statistics or categories directly side-by-side.

usage: Used to add information or arguments to support a point already made.
common_mistakes: Using 'furthermore' inside a sentence instead of at the start
example_sentences: The hotel is centrally located; furthermore, the prices are very reasonable.
Pollution is harming the planet. Furthermore, it threatens our future.
Furthermore, there is no evidence to support that claim.
The curriculum is outdated. Furthermore, it lacks practical application.
She is a talented athlete; furthermore, she excels academically.
native_notes: Avoid using this in speaking; it sounds robotic. Keep it for written assignments or formal presentations.

usage: Used to clarify, rephrase, or explain something said previously in simpler terms.
grammar_pattern: Clause, that is to say, + clarification
example_sentences: The project is labour-intensive; that is to say, it requires many workers.
We need to be more efficient, that is to say, reduce our unnecessary expenses.
His arguments were cryptic, that is to say, difficult to understand.
The company is downsizing, that is to say, they are laying off staff.
We are looking for a hybrid model; that is to say, part-time office and remote work.
native_notes: Very common in lectures to clarify academic terminology.

usage: Used to introduce an idea that is the exact opposite of what has just been mentioned.
example_sentences: Urban life is fast-paced; conversely, rural living is often quite tranquil.
High interest rates encourage saving; conversely, they discourage borrowing.
Some enjoy the heat; conversely, others prefer colder climates.
Young people are often tech-savvy; conversely, some seniors struggle with new devices.
Teamwork can boost speed; conversely, it might lead to slow group decisions.
native_notes: Use this only for direct binary opposites (e.g. cold vs hot, high vs low).

usage: Used to provide a specific example to support a claim made in the previous sentence.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to provide an actual example after
example_sentences: Urbanization is growing rapidly. To illustrate this, look at the recent population shifts in Tokyo.
Climate change is affecting agriculture. To illustrate this, many farmers are struggling with drought.
Technology has changed communication. To illustrate this, consider the rise of video conferencing.
The company is struggling financially. To illustrate this, they had to close three branches.
Public health has improved. To illustrate this, life expectancy has risen by five years.
native_notes: Sounds more academic than 'for example' and signals the listener that an explanatory example is coming.

usage: Used to add supplementary information or evidence to a point previously mentioned.
common_mistakes: In addition to study hard, I also...
In addition that it is expensive...
example_sentences: In addition to lower costs, solar energy is also better for the environment.
In addition to being a talented musician, she is a skilled painter.
The project faced delays in addition to a significant budget cut.
In addition to the main findings, the report highlights several minor issues.
He speaks French fluently in addition to his native English.
collocations: In addition to the fact that
native_notes: Use this to link two related ideas; it sounds more sophisticated than just saying 'and'.

usage: Used when moving to a conclusion or an action based on information previously mentioned.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the comma after the phrase
example_sentences: The city is becoming overcrowded. With this in mind, the council is planning new residential developments.
We are running out of time. With this in mind, let's focus on the most important points.
Prices are expected to rise. With this in mind, many families are starting to save more.
The data is quite old. With this in mind, we must interpret the results with caution.
Customer feedback was negative. With this in mind, the company overhauled its service strategy.
native_notes: A very useful transition in Writing Task 2 when you are linking a problem description to a suggested solution.

usage: Used to add an idea that is similar in nature to the one just mentioned.
common_mistakes: Using it to introduce a contrast
example_sentences: The government reduced income tax. In the same vein, they lowered corporate tax rates.
Primary education focuses on basic literacy. In the same vein, secondary schools prioritize critical thinking.
He criticized the lack of funding. In the same vein, his colleagues complained about the outdated equipment.
The artist experiments with light. In the same vein, her latest exhibition explores the concept of shadow.
Climate change affects agriculture. In the same vein, it threatens coastal ecosystems.
native_notes: This implies a deeper connection or structural similarity between two points than just 'also' or 'similarly'.

usage: Used to summarize or give a general opinion after looking at all aspects of a situation.
common_mistakes: Using it when you are only talking about one small specific detail
example_sentences: The weather was a bit unpredictable, but on the whole, we had a wonderful holiday.
On the whole, the students enjoyed the new curriculum despite some initial confusion.
The car has a few minor faults, but on the whole, it is a reliable vehicle.
On the whole, I think the changes will benefit the community in the long run.
While there were some delays, on the whole, the project was a success.
native_notes: Very common in IELTS Speaking Part 3 when you need to give a balanced summary of a topic before moving to a conclusion.

usage: Used to introduce a contrasting point, similar to 'nevertheless', but slightly more conversational.
common_mistakes: Using it at the start of a paragraph without context
example_sentences: The restaurant had great reviews. That being said, I found the service slow.
I enjoy my current job. That being said, I am looking for new challenges.
The film won many awards. That being said, it wasn't my personal favorite.
The evidence supports the theory. That being said, more research is needed.
It is a beautiful location. That being said, it is very difficult to access.
native_notes: A very popular connector in both spoken English and essays; highly versatile.
